title: Grounded Copilot: How Programmers Interact with Code-Generating Models
pub: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA 2023); held text is arXiv:2206.15000v3
author: Shraddha Barke · Michael B. James · Nadia Polikarpova

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source describes participant selection and a Copilot-assisted programming protocol but supplies no comparative baseline or findings on time, quality, learning, or verification costs. It therefore cannot establish whether AI saved or consumed time, though its attention to prior experience is relevant to evaluating heterogeneous workflow effects.
qs: To study participants using Copilot, we gave them a programming task to attempt with Copilot’s help.
Nine of the participants had used Copilot to varying degrees prior to the study.

st.t: Coding copilots: Completion speed excludes checking costs
st.an: The source accepts that completion-speed evidence and interaction/checking evidence measure different aspects of productivity, explicitly presenting its qualitative account as complementary to quantitative studies. It materially extends the cluster by distinguishing acceleration from exploration, documenting debugging burdens, and proposing continuous validation to reduce checking effort, while not estimating a comparative productivity effect.
qs: Further, instead of skewing quantitative answers to predefined research questions, we chose the grounded theory approach, with the general goal of finding patters in programmers’ behavior when they interact with Copilot; we believe this approach is complementary to the quantitative studies.
On the flip side, participants found it more difficult to spot an error in code generated by Copilot.

st.t: Coding workflow: Generation overhead limits productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s workflow-centred account and materially develops it by distinguishing acceleration from slower, prompting- and checking-intensive exploration. It also identifies concrete interface changes intended to reduce validation burdens, while not itself estimating a causal net-productivity effect.
qs: Our main                                          finding is that interactions with programming assistants are bimodal: in acceleration mode, the programmer                                          knows what to do next and uses Copilot to get there faster; in exploration mode, the programmer is unsure                                          how to proceed and uses Copilot to explore their options.

In exploration mode, the programmer is not sure how to proceed and uses Copilot to explore their options or get a starting point for the solution; interactions in this mode are slow and deliberate, and include explicit prompting and more extensive validation.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s copilot and jagged-capability framing and materially extends it with observed interaction modes and concrete design implications. It shows that task familiarity and user expertise shape whether AI accelerates known work or supports exploration, while difficult-to-detect errors make validation and mode-aware, selective assistance important. Its programming context and limited sample constrain direct generalisation to legal work.
qs: Our main                                          finding is that interactions with programming assistants are bimodal: in acceleration mode, the programmer                                          knows what to do next and uses Copilot to get there faster; in exploration mode, the programmer is unsure                                          how to proceed and uses Copilot to explore their options.
In the future, IDEs could couple code-generating models with some kind of always-on validation, in order to make the process of evaluating code suggestions less taxing for the developer.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious, task-centered framing: it treats code generation as programmer assistance rather than autonomous replacement and argues that adoption raises questions about which programming tasks benefit. However, it offers only prior technical benchmark results and does not assess whole-job productivity or durable skill formation.
qs: With this impressive performance, large code-generating models are quickly escaping research                                          labs to power industrial programming assistant tools, such as Github Copilot [Friedman 2021].

The growing adoption of these tools gives rise to questions about the nature of AI-assisted                                          programming: What kinds of tasks do programmers need assistance with?

kp.k: AI-assisted programming alternates between acceleration and exploration
kp.d: The authors develop a grounded theory of GitHub Copilot use in programming, rather than legal work. In acceleration mode, programmers know their next action and use suggestions to implement it; in exploration mode, they use suggestions to discover how to proceed. The authors liken these modes to fast and slow cognition, with programmers switching between them during a task. Exploration still involves human selection, examination and repair, not autonomous completion.
qs: In acceleration mode, a programmer uses Copilot to execute their planned code actions, by completing a logical unit of code or a comment.
In exploration mode, a programmer relies on Copilot to help them plan their code actions.
We found that programmers alternate between these two modes as they complete their task, fluidly switching from one mode to the other.

kp.k: Evidence describes interactions rather than comparative productivity gains
kp.d: The study observed 20 participants, comprising 15 from academia and 5 from industry; nine had prior Copilot experience. Participants attempted researcher-designed tasks across Python, Rust, Haskell and Java, including contributions to an existing codebase. Data collection and qualitative coding evolved together, with theoretical saturation reported at participant 20. Five YouTube and Twitch livestreams supplied additional qualitative support. This was not a controlled comparison of productivity with and without Copilot.
qs: We developed our theory through a user study with 20 participants (15 from academia and 5 from industry).
Nine of the participants had used Copilot to varying degrees prior to the study.
At the 20th participant, we could fit all existing data into our theory and no new data surprised us.
We gathered additional evidence in the form of five livestream videos to support our theory.

kp.d: The authors identify the ability to decompose a task into understood microtasks as the principal condition for acceleration. Understanding the algorithm appeared more important for entering this mode than language expertise or previous Copilot use, although more experienced language users and prior Copilot users spent larger proportions of interaction time accelerating. In the familiar Fibonacci portion of the Benford’s Law task, all four participants accelerated.
qs: We found that the main causal condition for a participant to end up in acceleration mode is being able to decompose the programming task into microtasks.
We define a microtask to be a participant-defined task with a well-understood and well-defined job.
All four participants were familiar with the Fibonacci sequence and knew how to make it efficient.

kp.d: During acceleration, participants preferred suggestions matching their current logical unit, which could range from a function call to an entire loop. Long suggestions were rejected or diverted attention into reviewing alternatives. P1, P6 and P15 had previously disabled Copilot and cited distraction from always-on suggestions as a factor. Quick acceptance commonly depended on expected keywords or control structures; repairs were generally limited to obvious small changes.
qs: When a programmer is focused on a logical unit of code, they want suggestions only for that unit.
In acceleration mode, long, multi-line suggestions are at best dismissed out of hand and at worst distract the programmer away from their flow.
Suggestions that are almost-correct were accepted if a small repair was obvious to the participant.

kp.d: Participants explored when unsure how to decompose unfamiliar tasks or when code behaved unexpectedly. Confidence and excitement about the model were associated with greater exploration, sometimes before participants attempted their own solution. The authors report that excessive enthusiasm could impede progress: P10 made the least progress among participants assigned the same task and acknowledged relying too heavily on Copilot. This illustrates a gap between user expectations and system capabilities, not a measured general effect on novice productivity.
qs: A participant’s level of confidence and excitement about code-generating models was highly correlated with whether and to which extent they would engage in exploration.
Sometimes, such excessive enthusiasm would get in the way of actually completing a task.
I was trying to get Copilot to do it for me, maybe I should have given smaller tasks to Copilot and done the rest myself instead of depending entirely on Copilot.

kp.k: Prompting changes commenting and information-seeking practices
kp.d: Exploration involved deliberate natural-language prompting, prompt revision and searches through multiple suggestions. Participants often distinguished comments written for Copilot from durable code documentation, sometimes removing them afterward. Some used Copilot instead of StackOverflow for syntax and unfamiliar API searches. This could help participants use an API without necessarily deepening their understanding, as P5 explicitly reported.
qs: Participants seem to distinguish between comments made for themselves and Copilot.
They would rewrite comments with more relevant information if the suggestions did not match their expectations, engaging in a conversation with Copilot.
what would have been a StackOverflow search, Copilot pretty much gave that to me.
It definitely helped me understand how best to use the API. I feel like my actual understanding of [the socket or crypto library] is not better but I was able to use them effectively.

kp.k: Multiple suggestions support exploration but introduce cognitive biases
kp.d: Participants selected and combined snippets, searched for API patterns, and treated repeated patterns across suggestions as signs of model confidence. The authors also observed cognitive overload when comparing alternatives and anchoring on the first suggestion, including a belief that suggestions were ranked by suitability. These are observations about users’ confidence judgments, not evidence that repetition or ordering reliably indicates correctness.
qs: Participants took part of a solution from the multi-suggestion pane or combined code from different solutions in the pane.
Participants seemed to think that repetition implied Copilot was more confident about the suggestion.
We observed participants believe that suggestions were ranked and that the top suggestion must be closest to their intent (P18).
Seeing the code in context of where it’s going to be was way more valuable than seeing it in a separate pane where I have to draw all these additional connections.

kp.k: Human checking varies with interaction mode and tooling
kp.d: The authors use validation broadly to mean increasing confidence that generated code matches intent. Acceleration commonly involved rapid pattern-based inspection, while exploration involved closer examination, execution, documentation and static analysis. Static-analysis use was not timed because it ran automatically in the background. Execution occupied a larger share of validation time during acceleration; the authors explain that exploratory code was often incomplete and that detailed examination consumed more time. Participants’ reliance on type checkers is reported as their practice, not proof of semantic correctness.
qs: Programmers would validate Copilot’s suggestions more carefully in exploration mode as compared to acceleration.
Their validation strategies included code examination, code execution (or testing), relying on IDE-integrated static analysis (e.g. a type checker), and looking up documentation.
A somewhat surprising result is that execution seems to be more prevalent during acceleration.
One reason for this is that during exploration the code is often incomplete and cannot be executed.

kp.k: Generated drafts shift work toward review and repair
kp.d: During exploration, participants accepted imperfect code, retained snippets for later use, and stripped suggestions down to control structures. P5 described the attraction of reviewing rather than writing code. However, generated code could be harder to debug because users understood it less well. P9 failed to complete a task after a suggestion opened a file read-only; rather than locating that error, they pursued an unrelated file-flush operation.
qs: It’s nice to have code to review instead of write
Some participants were able to complete most of their task by accepting a large block of code and then slowly breaking it down.
On the flip side, participants found it more difficult to spot an error in code generated by Copilot.
Copilot’s suggestion opened a file in read-only mode, causing the program to fail when attempting to write.

kp.k: Exploration consumed more observed interaction time
kp.d: Across participants, exploration accounted for 248.6 minutes versus 104.7 minutes for acceleration. Prior users spent less time exploring and more accelerating than first-time users, while unfamiliar APIs pushed participants toward exploration irrespective of expertise or prior use. The authors found no noticeable Python–Rust difference in total interaction time or mode ratio; Haskell and Java had too few observations for conclusions. They report code prompts at 71.4% and context prompts at 15.2% in acceleration, and comment prompting at 57.2% in exploration versus 13.1% in acceleration. These are descriptive study results, not estimates of time saved.
qs: The total amount of study time spent by all participants interacting with Copilot in exploration mode (248.6 minutes) is more than twice that in acceleration mode (104.7 minutes).
Given roughly the same overall time, prior users spend less time exploring (and more time accelerating) than novice users.
We did not identify any noticeable differences in either total interaction time or ratio of acceleration to exploration between Python and Rust.
In exploration mode, participants intentionally prompt with comments a lot more than in acceleration mode (57.2% vs 13.1%).

kp.k: Recommended interfaces preserve control and reduce checking burdens
kp.d: The authors propose, rather than experimentally establish, benefits from mode-aware assistance: short, high-confidence suggestions during acceleration and better comparison tools during exploration. Other recommendations include explicit control over model context, isolated prompting scratchpads, expert prompt syntax, cross-language translation, and code skeletons with holes. They also recommend coupling generation with always-on checking, such as property-based testing or live displays of runtime values.
qs: We conjecture that the user experience could be improved if the tool were aware of the current interaction mode and adjusted its behavior accordingly.
Based on these observations, future tools could give programmers ways to customize the context.
Based on our observations, future tools should mind how large code blocks can break the user’s natural development flow, instead offering code holes for users to fill in when ready.
In the future, IDEs could couple code-generating models with some kind of always-on validation, in order to make the process of evaluating code suggestions less taxing for the developer.

kp.k: Sampling and rapidly changing technology limit generalisation
kp.d: The authors caution that researcher-designed tasks, unfamiliar codebases and study time pressure may affect interaction patterns. The work focused on code authorship rather than the broader software-engineering lifecycle. The small, academia-heavy sample and 11 first-time Copilot users limit representativeness; established users may also have developed habits from earlier technical-preview versions. The study did not track changes over longer periods, and the authors acknowledge that technological advances could supersede its findings.
qs: Our participants worked on tasks of our design, as opposed to their own projects.
Moreover, our tasks focused only on code authorship, as opposed to refactoring, testing, debugging, or other common aspects of software engineering.
11 of our participants had not used Copilot before the study, and hence might not be representative of regular users of the tool.
Finally, the research on code-generating models is progressing very rapidly, and it is possible that new technological breakthroughs will soon render our findings obsolete.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Barke, James and Polikarpova claim that AI-assisted programming has two alternating modes: accelerating a known solution and exploring how to solve an unfamiliar problem.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of GitHub Copilot, not legal services. The authors describe acceleration as intelligent autocomplete that helps execute an already-planned action with little interruption. Exploration helps programmers identify APIs, algorithms or starting points, but requires more deliberate prompting and checking. These are observations and grounded-theory hypotheses about human augmentation, not findings of autonomous programmer replacement or a measured overall productivity gain.

pts.k: The authors claim that Copilot can shift work from writing code and searching externally toward prompting, selecting, reviewing and repairing generated code.
pts.d: In exploration, participants used natural-language comments, compared multiple suggestions, retained useful fragments and edited larger blocks. Some used Copilot in place of StackOverflow searches. Participant P5 described a shift toward code review and reported being able to use unfamiliar APIs without a corresponding deeper understanding. The authors also observed changes to commenting practices, including writing prompts before code and deleting prompt-only comments afterward.

pts.k: The authors claim that generated suggestions can impose distraction, comprehension and debugging costs, and that excessive reliance can hinder task completion.
pts.d: Long suggestions interrupted acceleration or were rejected immediately; three participants cited distracting suggestions as a reason they had previously disabled Copilot. Multiple alternatives could cause cognitive overload and anchoring on the first suggestion. Participants sometimes treated repeated patterns across suggestions as evidence of reliability; the study records this user belief rather than establishing its validity. P10 attributed limited progress to excessive reliance, while P9 failed to complete a task after struggling to diagnose subtly incorrect generated code.

pts.k: AI assistance leaves substantial human verification work, with the form of checking depending on the interaction mode.
pts.d: The authors call this work validation: checking generated code against the user's intent. In acceleration, programmers often triaged suggestions by matching expected keywords or control structures. In exploration, they examined code more carefully, consulted documentation, executed code or relied on static analysis. Execution represented a greater share of measured validation time in acceleration, whereas examination took substantially more absolute time in exploration. These findings concern checking behavior, not proof that accepted code was correct.

pts.k: The authors predict that mode-aware interfaces and better verification support could improve future programming assistants.
pts.d: These are explicitly prospective recommendations, not tested outcomes. Proposed changes include shorter, higher-confidence suggestions during acceleration; better comparison of alternatives during exploration; control over prompt context; skeletal suggestions with holes; and always-on testing or live runtime feedback. The authors also suggest investigating cross-language prompting and translation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central evidence is an iterative qualitative study of 20 programmers, supplemented by descriptive timing analysis and five livestreams.
pts.d: The sample contained 15 academics and five industry participants; nine had prior Copilot experience. Participants attempted researcher-designed tasks in Python, Rust, Haskell or Java, with a core task lasting approximately 20–40 minutes within an hour-long session. Recordings, think-aloud accounts and interviews were coded through Straussian grounded theory. After developing the theory, the researchers re-coded the videos using a fixed codebook and examined five publicly available livestreams for corroboration. Total observed Copilot interaction time was 248.6 minutes in exploration and 104.7 minutes in acceleration. These durations describe interaction modes, not time saved relative to unaided programming. The study deliberately did not use a comparative task-completion design.

pts.k: Model-capability claims in the introduction rely on cited external benchmarks, not this user study.
pts.d: The authors cite Chen et al. (2021) for Codex solving 30–70% of novel Python problems and Li et al. (2022) for AlphaCode ranking in the top 54.3% among 5,000 competitive programmers. These claims motivate studying AI programming assistants; they do not establish real-world productivity gains, worker substitution or legal-domain performance. Future interface recommendations instead derive from observed behaviors and participant requests, sometimes supported by related tool-design literature.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe early Copilot use in the held October 2022 manuscript; future improvements have no specified delivery date.
pts.d: The supplied version is arXiv:2206.15000v3, dated 31 October 2022, with the document header identifying OOPSLA 2023 publication. The observations concern the then-current Codex-powered assistant and include technical-preview users. Acceleration depends especially on knowing how to decompose a task; unfamiliar APIs, uncertain algorithms or unexpected behavior encourage exploration. More experienced language users and prior Copilot users spent more time accelerating. No noticeable Python–Rust difference was identified, and the other languages had too few observations for conclusions. The authors caution that short, researcher-designed authorship tasks, an academia-heavy sample, novice-user effects and rapid model changes limit generalization. They did not establish longitudinal changes in work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are programmers with differing task knowledge and experience, and designers of programming assistants and IDEs.
pts.d: Programmers who understand a task can use suggestions to reduce routine typing and API recall. Those facing unfamiliar work can obtain starting points but must invest in prompting, comprehension, checking and repair. First-time users may overestimate the tool and become over-reliant; experienced users more often accelerate through familiar work. Tool designers are urged to preserve flow, support exploration and reduce verification burden. The paper does not claim effects on lawyer employment, legal markets, client costs, staffing structures or access to justice, and it does not quantify programming employment or wage effects.
